opts: What is needed to make things happen
quiz.why: Energy is what is needed to make something move, light up, heat up or make a sound. Electricity and food carry energy, but they are not energy itself.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT an example of energy at work?
opts: A drawing lying in a drawer
quiz.why: The drawing in the drawer is not moving, lighting up, heating up or making a sound. The others are all energy at work.

quiz.p: Kavya's mixie grinds chutney and hums. Which forms of energy come out of it?
opts: Movement, sound and a little heat
quiz.why: The blades move, the motor hums and the mixie gets a little warm. One machine often passes energy on in more than one form.

quiz.p: Lakshmi lies in bed with a torch. The torch's energy came from
opts: the light switch on the wall
quiz.why: The cells hold stored energy. The bulb changes it into light.

quiz.p: Where did the energy in a plate of rice and sambar first come from?
quiz.why: Rice and dal plants caught sunlight and stored its energy in their grains. The stove only heated the food.

quiz.p: Wind turbines at Muppandal turn in the wind. What makes the wind blow?
opts: The Sun warming some places more than others
quiz.why: The Sun warms the land and the sea by different amounts. Warm air rises and cooler air moves in. That moving air is the wind.

quiz.p: Meenakshi drops a marble into atta from 20 cm and then from 80 cm. Which change made the second crater wider?
opts: The marble landed faster, with more energy
quiz.why: In a fair test only the height changes. From higher up, the marble lands faster, with more movement energy, so it digs a wider crater.

quiz.p: In the Atta Crater Test, why do we drop the marble 3 times from each height?
opts: Because one try can be a fluke
quiz.why: Results change a little each time. Three tries show what usually happens.

quiz.p: Where did the energy of the falling marble come from?
opts: From the arm that lifted it up
quiz.why: Lifting the marble took energy from the arm. That energy was stored in the lifted marble and became movement as it fell.

quiz.p: A spinning top slows down and stops. What happened to its movement energy?
opts: It passed into the floor and the air as a little warmth
It went back into the hand
quiz.why: Energy is never destroyed. Rubbing on the floor and the air passed it on as a tiny bit of warmth.

opts: Energy can be made from nothing
Energy is never made or destroyed, only passed on
Energy is always destroyed in the end
quiz.why: This is the conservation of energy. Every careful measurement agrees with it.

quiz.p: Willem 's Gravesande, a Dutch scientist, dropped brass balls into soft clay in 1722. A ball that landed twice as fast made a dent
quiz.why: Twice as fast gave about four times the dent. This showed that a moving thing's energy grows much faster than its speed.

quiz.p: Émilie du Châtelet was a French scientist. What did she do with 's Gravesande's results?
opts: She explained in her physics book that they showed a faster ball carries much more energy
She built the first wind turbine
quiz.why: In her book of 1740, she explained that the clay dents agreed with Gottfried Leibniz: twice the speed means four times the effect.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, looks around her kitchen. Sort each thing by what its energy is doing.
items.a: see items
items.why: Each thing is sorted by its main job. Many do more than one: the mixie also hums, and the tubelight also gets a little warm. A strong answer notices that one thing can pass its energy on in more than one form.

items.p: Energy is what is needed to make something ____.
items.why: Anything that moves, lights up, heats up or makes a sound needs energy. 'Work' and 'move' are also fine answers, if the child explains them.

items.p: Divya switches on a torch in the dark. Where does the torch get its energy?
items.why: The cells, often called batteries, hold stored energy. Electricity carries it to the bulb, which gives out light. Picking 'the bulb' is common, because that is where the light appears. But the bulb only changes the energy into light.

items.p: Lakshmi says, 'A ball sitting still on a high shelf has no energy, because it is not moving.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A ball high on a shelf has stored energy, because it was lifted up. If it falls, that stored energy becomes movement energy. A strong answer says what would happen if the ball fell.

items.p: Match each thing to the source of its energy.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every thing gets its energy from somewhere. A strong answer could also say where the crow's food got the energy: from plants, and so from the Sun.

items.p: Meenakshi drops the same marble into atta, first from 20 cm and then from 80 cm. What will she see?
opts: There is no crater from 80 cm
items.why: From higher up, the marble lands faster and carries more movement energy. That energy pushes more atta aside, so the crater is wider. This is what the Atta Crater Test showed.

items.p: In the Atta Crater Test, why did the marble from 80 cm make a louder thud than the marble from 20 cm?
items.a: It fell from higher, so it was moving faster when it landed. It had more movement energy, so more of its energy became sound.
items.why: A strong answer links three things: the height, the speed when it landed, and the energy that became sound.

items.p: Put the energy chain for a ceiling fan in order, starting at the Sun.
items: the Sun warms the land and sea
electricity carries the energy along wires
the wind turns a wind turbine
a: the Sun warms the land and sea
the wind turns a wind turbine
electricity carries the energy along wires
items.why: The Sun's heat makes the wind. The wind turns the turbine, which makes electricity. Electricity carries the energy to the fan. A strong answer could add that some fans get their energy from coal or water instead.

items.p: Draw a torch. Show with arrows where the energy starts, where it travels, and what it turns into.
items.a: Arrows from the cells, along the wire or metal strip, to the bulb, with light coming out and a little heat.
items.why: A strong drawing starts the energy in the cells, not the bulb, and shows that the bulb gives out light and a little heat.
items.art: A blank outline of a torch.

items.p: Three of these get their energy from food. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A solar panel gets its energy straight from sunlight. The child, the crow and the ant all get their energy from food. That food got its energy from sunlight too, a step further back.

items.p: Sneha puts one tumbler of water in the sun and one in the shade. After an hour, the sunny one is warmer. Why?
opts: Sunlight carries energy, which turned into heat in the water
The sunny tumbler had more water
Shade makes water colder by adding cold
items.why: Sunlight carries energy from the Sun. When it lands on the water and the tumbler, it turns into heat. Shade does not add cold. It just lets less sunlight in.

items.p: Arjun says, 'My energy is my own. It doesn't come from anywhere.' Write two sentences to tell him where his energy came from.
items.a: Your energy came from the food you ate, like idli or rice. That food got its energy from plants, which caught it from sunlight.
items.why: A strong answer goes back at least two steps: from Arjun to food, and from food to plants or the Sun.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi argue after a game of football. They are both very tired.

views.says: We used up all our energy. It's gone.
Energy can never be used up. It just went somewhere else.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you know about where energy goes. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Revathi that energy is never destroyed: it passed into the ball, sounds, and mostly warmth spreading into the air. It gives Anjali her due: the energy is gone from their bodies, in a form they can't use again, so they need to eat and rest.
items.why: Both friends see part of the truth. Scientists agree with Revathi about the total. Anjali is right about what she feels: the useful energy in her body is lower.

items.p: Label the drawing of a pressure cooker on a gas stove with these words: fuel, heat, steam pushes the whistle, sound.
items.a: fuel on the gas cylinder, heat at the flame, steam pushes the whistle at the top, sound beside the whistle.
items.why: A strong answer follows the energy in order: from the fuel, to heat, to steam pushing the whistle up, to the sound.
items.art: A pressure cooker on a gas stove with a gas cylinder underneath, with four blank labels.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Hyderabad, says, 'Electricity is a source of energy, like the Sun.' What is a better way to say it?
opts: Electricity carries energy from a power station to our homes
Electricity is made inside the switch
Electricity is a kind of fuel we burn
items.why: Electricity carries energy along wires. The energy came from a power station, which got it from coal, gas, wind, sunlight, falling water or uranium.

items.p: Priya drops a marble into atta from 20 cm, then from 80 cm, four times as high. The second crater is
opts: wider, but much less than four times as wide
items.why: The higher drop gives the marble more energy, so the crater is wider. But a crater twice as wide must push aside much more atta than twice as much. So the width grows much more slowly than the height. In made-up results, 4.5 cm grew to only about 6.5 cm.

items.p: In the Atta Crater Test, we smoothed the atta and used the same marble every time. Why did that matter?
items.a: So that the only thing that changed was the height. Then any difference in the craters must come from the height.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of a fair test: change one thing, keep everything else the same.

items.p: When a spinning top slows down and stops, its energy has been destroyed.
items.why: False. The top's movement energy passed into the floor and the air through rubbing, as a tiny bit of warmth. Energy is never destroyed, only passed on.

items.p: A coconut falls from a tall tree and lands with a thud. Put what happens to the energy in order.
items: the coconut lands, and the energy becomes sound and pushes the soil
the coconut speeds up as it falls
the coconut hangs high up with stored energy
the coconut lets go of the tree
a: the coconut hangs high up with stored energy
the coconut lets go of the tree
the coconut speeds up as it falls
the coconut lands, and the energy becomes sound and pushes the soil
items.why: Stored energy from height becomes movement energy as the coconut speeds up. When it lands, the energy passes into sound, the moving soil and a little warmth.

items.p: A sleeping cat is not moving, lighting up or making a sound. Is she using energy? Explain.
items.a: Yes. She is breathing, her heart is beating, and her body stays warm. All of that uses energy from her food.
items.why: A strong answer names at least one thing inside the cat's body that needs energy, such as her heartbeat or keeping warm.

items.p: In the Spinning Paper Snake activity, a paper spiral turns above a lit diya. Which energy change makes it turn?
items.why: The flame heats the air. Warm air rises and pushes on the spiral, so heat energy becomes movement energy.

items.p: Match each energy change to where it happens.
pairs: stored energy in food into movement
a balcony floor in the sun
a marble landing on a steel plate
stored energy in gas into heat
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In each case, energy changes from one form to another. A strong answer could also name the heat that nearly always comes out too.

items.p: The rule that energy is never made and never destroyed is called the ____ of energy.
items.why: Conservation means keeping. The total amount of energy is always kept the same.

items.p: Draw an energy chain from the Sun to a lit diya. Draw at least 4 steps, with an arrow between each.
items.a: For example: the Sun, a sesame or groundnut plant, oil pressed from the seeds, the diya flame giving light and heat.
items.why: A strong drawing has steps in the right order, and each step really gets its energy from the step before.
items.art: A blank strip with 4 empty boxes and arrows between them.

items.p: Three of these energy sources came from the Sun. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Uranium was made in stars before the Sun was born. Wind is moved by the Sun's heat, coal came from ancient plants that grew in sunlight, and the Sun's heat lifted the water into the clouds before it fell as rain.

items.p: Two cousins in Mysuru argue about a ball on a high shelf.

views.says: The ball has energy right now. It's stored, ready to fall.
The ball has no energy until it falls. Energy only shows when something happens.

items.ask: Which cousin do you agree with? Use the Atta Crater Test or the water bottle lift as evidence. Then say what the other cousin has right.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Tanvi: lifting the ball took energy, which is stored, and it comes out when it falls, as in the atta craters. It gives Ishaan his due: we only see energy when something happens, and nothing shows while the ball sits still.
items.why: Scientists call Tanvi's idea stored energy, or potential energy. Ishaan is right that we notice energy only by what it does.

items.p: Nandini's mother gives her two bulbs that give the same light. One gets very hot and one stays only a little warm. Which one passes less energy on as heat?
opts: The one that gets very hot
The one that stays only a little warm
Both pass on the same heat
items.why: Both make the same light, but the hot one also passes a lot of energy on as heat. The cooler one, usually an LED, turns more of its energy into light. So it needs less electricity for the same light.

items.p: A rock falls in the hills and starts a small landslide that knocks down many more rocks. Where did all that energy come from?
items.a: Each rock had stored energy from being high up on the hill. The first rock started the fall, but each rock brought its own stored energy as it fell.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the first rock did not give all the energy. Like the falling book in the Chain Reaction Bell, every lifted thing brings its own stored energy.

items.p: Label the energy changes in a phone: battery, light from the screen, sound from the speaker, heat.
items.a: battery at the bottom, light at the screen, sound at the speaker, heat where the phone feels warm on its back.
items.why: A strong answer starts the energy in the battery and shows it leaving as light, sound and heat.
items.art: A drawing of a phone, front and back, with four blank labels.

items.p: Sort these by where their energy came from.
items: a hot spring deep in the Earth
items.a: see items
items.why: Food, wind and gas all trace back to sunlight. Nuclear power uses uranium, and hot springs get heat from deep inside the Earth. A strong answer can explain one 'from the Sun' chain.

items.p: In 1722, Willem 's Gravesande dropped brass balls into soft clay. A ball that landed twice as fast made a dent about four times as deep. Why was that a surprise to people at the time?
items.a: Many scientists thought a ball twice as fast would hit twice as hard. The dent four times as deep showed that a faster ball carries much more energy than they thought.
items.why: A strong answer names the old idea (twice as fast, twice as hard) and says what the dents showed instead.

items.p: Scientists in Europe argued about this for many years in the 1700s.

views.says: What a moving ball carries is its weight times its speed. Twice as fast, twice as much.

views.who: Émilie du Châtelet, a French scientist
views.says: The clay dents show that what a moving ball carries is weight times speed times speed. Twice as fast, four times as much.

items.ask: Which side do the clay dents support? Then say what the other side had right.
items.a: The dents support du Châtelet: twice the speed gave four times the dent. But the other side was not simply wrong. Weight times speed is also a real quantity, which scientists now call momentum. It tells how hard a thing is to stop in a given time. Both sides were measuring something true, but different.
items.why: This was a real argument. A strong answer uses the evidence for du Châtelet, and also sees that the Descartes side had found a different true quantity.

items.p: Kavya drops a marble from 20 cm. To make it land twice as fast, from what height should she drop it?
items.why: To land twice as fast, a falling thing must fall from four times the height. 4 times 20 cm is 80 cm. This is because energy grows with speed times speed. Twice the speed needs four times the energy, and four times the energy needs four times the height.

items.p: We say a cell is 'used up' when the torch stops working. Explain what really happened to its energy.
items.a: The energy was carried by electricity to the bulb. The bulb turned it into light and a little heat. The light landed on walls and turned into warmth. So the energy spread out into the room as a tiny bit of warmth. It is still there, but too spread out to use.
items.why: A strong answer follows the energy step by step until it spreads out as warmth, and says why spread-out warmth is hard to use again.

items.p: A clever enough machine could keep running for ever without any new energy.
items.why: False. Every real machine passes some energy on as heat through rubbing, so it slows down unless new energy is put in. Many inventors have tried for hundreds of years, and none has worked.

items.p: Design a machine that uses falling water to ring a bell. Draw it, and label where the energy starts and every change it goes through.
items.a: For example: a bottle of water on a high shelf, a pipe, a small paper wheel turned by the falling water, a string on the wheel that pulls a spoon against a tumbler. Labels: stored energy from height, movement, sound.
items.why: A strong design starts with water high up, uses its fall to turn or push something, and ends in sound. Labels follow the energy in order.
items.art: A blank page with a bell drawn at the bottom right.

items.p: A resting child gives out about as much heat as an old 60 watt bulb. Where does this heat come from?
opts: From the air around the child
From the energy in the food the child ate
From the Sun shining on the child right now
items.why: Your body uses energy from food all the time, even while resting, to keep your heart beating and your body working. Much of it comes out as heat. That is why a room full of people gets warm.

items.p: Revathi says, 'Since energy is never destroyed, we don't need to save electricity.' What would you tell her?
items.a: The total energy stays the same, but after we use it, it is spread out as warmth that we can't use again. Making new electricity often means burning coal or building power stations. So saving electricity means needing less of that.
items.why: A strong answer separates the total amount of energy, which never changes, from useful energy, which runs down.

items.p: Match each Indian power station to the source of its energy.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Muppandal has hundreds of wind turbines, Idukki uses water stored behind a dam, Kudankulam is a nuclear power station, and Pavagada is a huge solar park. All but Kudankulam trace back to the Sun.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that gives most of its energy as light to the one that gives the least. All three use the same electricity.
items.why: An LED turns much of its energy into light. An old filament bulb turns only a small part into light and most into heat. A heater is made to turn nearly all of it into heat, with only a little red glow.

items.p: Label the parts of a falling marble's journey: stored energy, speeding up, movement energy at the bottom, crater and sound.
items.a: stored energy at the top where it is held, speeding up along the fall, movement energy just before it lands, crater and sound at the atta.
items.why: A strong answer follows the energy from stored, to movement, to the crater and sound.
items.art: A marble at three points on a dotted line from a hand down to a tray of atta, with four blank labels.

items.p: The unit scientists use to measure energy is called the ____. It is about the energy needed to lift a small apple one metre.
items.why: The joule is named after James Joule, who measured how work makes heat in the 1840s.

items.p: The Sun will one day run out of hydrogen to join into helium. What would happen on Earth if the Sun stopped shining? Follow at least two energy chains.
items.a: Plants could not make food, so animals and people would run out of food. Without the Sun's heat, there would be no wind and no rain filling the dams. The Earth would get very cold.
items.why: A strong answer follows at least two chains, such as food and wind or rain, and sees how much depends on sunlight. (The Sun has billions of years left.)

items.p: Sort these by whether the energy is stored or happening now.
items: a coconut high on the tree
items.a: see items
items.why: Stored energy waits until something lets it out. Moving, sounding, lighting and heating are energy happening now. A strong answer could say what would let each stored one out.

items.p: Ishita runs up four floors of stairs in her building in Pune. At the top she feels hot and out of breath. Why does she feel hot?
opts: Her muscles passed on energy from her food, and much of it came out as heat
Running makes cold air leave her body
items.why: Her muscles used energy from her food to lift her up four floors. Much of that energy came out as heat, as it nearly always does when energy changes form. That is why she feels hot. Picking 'cold air leaves her body' mixes up heat and cold: heat is the energy that moves, not cold.

applications: Power stations turn wind, falling water, sunlight, coal, gas or uranium into electricity for homes.
Engineers work out how much energy a moving car or train carries, to design brakes and crash barriers.
Doctors and dieticians measure the energy in food, to help people eat enough.
Solar panels on roofs and at airports, such as Kochi, turn sunlight into electricity.
LED bulbs are used to give the same light with less energy wasted as heat.
Builders use energy stored in a lifted weight: a pile driver drops a heavy block to hammer posts into the ground.

open_questions.why_open: Scientists can count it very exactly and it always adds up, but nobody can say what it is underneath.
The universe is spreading out faster and faster. Scientists call whatever is causing this 'dark energy', but nobody knows what it is.

open_questions.q: Does the whole universe add up to zero energy?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists think the energy of all the stuff is balanced by gravity. Others say the question has no clear answer.

open_questions.q: How can we store sunlight cheaply for the night?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries work but cost a lot. Scientists are testing new batteries, pumped water and making fuels from sunlight.

ask_kids: What made something happen in the kitchen this morning? Where did its energy come from?
Is the energy from your lunch still in you? Where will it go?

maths.problem: In the Atta Crater Test, Kavya's three craters from 20 cm were 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm wide. What was the average width?
maths.explain: Add the three widths: 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 cm. Share 15 among 3 tries: 15 divided by 3 is 5. So the average width is 5 cm. The average is one number that stands for all three tries.
maths.why_maths: Each drop gives a slightly different crater. The average gives one fair number for each height, so we can compare heights.
maths.context: This is about the Atta Crater Test, where you drop a marble into atta from different heights and measure the craters.

maths.problem: Kavya dropped the marble from 20 cm, 40 cm and 80 cm. What is the pattern in the heights? What would the next height be?
maths.answer: Each height is double the one before. The next would be 160 cm.
maths.explain: 20 doubled is 40. 40 doubled is 80. 80 doubled is 160. 160 cm is taller than most grown-ups, so a grown-up would need to stand on a stool.
maths.why_maths: Doubling the height each time makes the change in the craters easier to see than adding a little each time.
maths.context: This is about the three drop heights in the Atta Crater Test.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results: from 20 cm the crater was 4.5 cm wide, and from 80 cm it was 6.5 cm wide. The height went up 4 times. Did the width go up 4 times? How much wider was it?
maths.answer: No. It was only 2 cm wider, much less than 4 times.
maths.explain: 4 times 4.5 cm would be 18 cm. The real crater was 6.5 cm. 6.5 minus 4.5 is 2, so it was 2 cm wider. The marble had 4 times the energy, but a wider crater must move much more atta. So the width grows slowly.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the change in height with the change in width shows a surprise: four times the energy does not mean four times the width.
maths.context: This is about the Atta Crater Test. The numbers are made up, but are like what families find.

maths.problem: Lifting a 100 gram apple 1 metre takes about 1 joule. How many joules does it take to lift 5 such apples 1 metre? What about lifting 1 apple 3 metres?
maths.explain: Each apple lifted 1 metre takes about 1 joule, so 5 apples take 5 times as much: 5 joules. One apple lifted 3 metres is like 3 lifts of 1 metre each: 3 joules. More weight or more height means more energy.
maths.why_maths: Energy can be counted. Multiplying shows that lifting more, or higher, stores more energy, as in the bottle lift.
maths.context: This is about the joule, the unit scientists use to measure energy.

maths.problem: In Pass the Sunshine, the yellow ball started with 6 sheets. One sheet was torn off into the HEAT bowl at each of the 5 passes. How many sheets were left in the ball? How many in the bowl? How many altogether?
maths.answer: 1 sheet in the ball, 5 in the bowl, 6 altogether.
maths.explain: 6 sheets minus 5 torn off leaves 1. The bowl has 5. 1 + 5 = 6, the same as at the start. Nothing was lost: it was only moved to the bowl.
maths.why_maths: Adding the two parts back together checks the big idea of the game: the total energy stays the same.
maths.context: This is about the game Pass the Sunshine, where a ball of yellow paper is passed along an energy chain.

roots.context: We have learned that energy makes things happen, and that it is passed on from one thing to another. Now we ask what energy tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The marble dropped from higher dug a wider crater and made a louder thud. The extra energy came from your arm, which lifted it higher. Your arm's energy came from food, and the food's energy from sunlight. So that crater in the atta was dug, step by step, with sunlight.
deep_truth.habit: We speak of moving, lighting, heating and sounding as separate happenings, and we think each thing makes its own energy. But nothing makes the energy it uses. It is passed on from somewhere else, and you can follow it back, step by step.
deep_truth.evidence: From 80 cm the marble made a wider crater and a louder thud than from 20 cm. Lifting the water bottle above your head ten times tired your arm more than lifting it to your knee. More energy went in when you lifted higher, and more came out in the crater and the sound.

three.who_am_i: Every move you make, and the warmth of your body, runs on energy from your food. That energy was sunlight caught by plants.
three.what_is_life: A plant catches sunlight and stores the Sun's energy in food. Every animal, you too, lives on that store, passed from one living thing to the next.
three.what_is_this_world: Wind, rain, rivers and the food on your plate are all moved by the Sun's energy. Almost everything that happens on Earth starts with sunlight.

roots.thread: Moving, lighting, heating and sounding look like four different things. Underneath, they are one thing, energy, showing up in four ways. It is never made fresh by the thing that uses it. It passes from the Sun to a leaf, to a grain, to your arm, to a falling marble, to a thud, and the total never changes. So all the different happenings of a day are one supply of energy, passed from hand to hand.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. It only passes on and changes form. This is the conservation of energy.
Almost all the energy used by life on Earth comes from the Sun, caught by plants and tiny sea life. A few deep-sea communities live on chemical energy from inside the Earth instead.
What energy is, underneath, nobody can say. Richard Feynman said that we have no knowledge of what energy is, only rules for counting it.

other_view.view: Energy is a number that scientists work out, and it stays the same when nothing gets in or out. Saying that sunlight dug the crater is a pleasant way of telling the story, but the number itself tells us nothing about meaning or oneness. It is simply a useful tool for predicting what will happen.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Changes made: the atta must be at least 3 cm deep, or a marble from 80 cm hits the bottom and the craters stop growing, so the materials ask for a container 4 cm deep and about half a kilo of atta. A dusting of ragi flour, cocoa or haldi on top makes the thrown atta and the crater edge easy to see and measure. The child measures the hole, not the splash lines, with a ruler held just above it. The crater from four times the height is wider but usually far less than four times as wide, so the unit says so and turns it into a question instead of promising a big jump. A marble is too light for a child to feel the extra effort of lifting higher, so a 1 litre water bottle lift was added. Sunshine in a Tumbler needs direct sun for a full hour: the step says to check where the sunny patch moves, and to try another day if it is cloudy. A fever thermometer only reads from about 35 degrees, so it is ruled out. The paper snake needs a diya or tea light, a grown-up, and at least 20 cm between flame and paper. Both games work for one child alone. Marbles are a choking risk for children under 3. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1600s, scientists argued about what a moving ball carries with it. René Descartes, a French thinker, said it was the ball's size times its speed. So a ball moving twice as fast should hit twice as hard. In 1686, Gottfried Leibniz, a German thinker, disagreed. He said it was the ball's weight times its speed times its speed again. Then twice as fast would hit four times as hard. In 1722, Willem 's Gravesande, a Dutch scientist, tested it. He dropped brass balls into soft clay from different heights and measured the dents. A ball that landed twice as fast did not make a dent twice as deep. It made a dent about four times as deep. Émilie du Châtelet, a French scientist, saw what this meant. In her physics book of 1740, she explained that the clay dents agreed with Leibniz. Her book was read and argued about across Europe. In 1807, Thomas Young, an English scientist, began to call this quantity energy. Your Atta Crater Test is a small copy of the clay test.
how_we_found_out.who: Willem 's Gravesande, a Dutch scientist, and Émilie du Châtelet, a French scientist, testing an idea of Gottfried Leibniz
how_we_found_out.when: 1686 (Leibniz's idea), 1722 (the clay test) and 1740 (du Châtelet's book)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists, following Descartes, thought a ball moving twice as fast carries twice as much and hits twice as hard. The clay dents showed that twice as fast does about four times as much.
